title: protected and access control

youtube.title: C++ public, protected and private Explained | C++ Programming EP 63
youtube.description: In this episode you will use the protected label, read the access table and choose the right label, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 protected and access control · 1:15 A protected member · 2:08 Who can reach what · 2:49 Second program · 4:06 Recap · 4:36 Bug of the Day · 5:30 Challenge · 6:00 Next episode

thumbnail.visual: big text "PROTECTED" in tomato on pastel blue; Xecxec next to three doors labelled public, protected and private; thin black border and drop shadow.
thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to three doors labelled public, protected and private

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we meet the third access label. It sits between public and private, and it is made for inheritance.

scenes.onScreen: "protected and access control": numbered lines (1. Public is open to everyone; 2. Protected is open to the class and its children; 3. Private is open to the class only) and an analogy card: a family house: the street sees the gate, the family sees the hall, only you see your room
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: Public members are open to everyone. Private members are open to the class only. Protected members are open to the class and to its derived classes, but not to the outside. Choose the strictest label that works. Think of a family house. The street sees the gate. The family sees the hall. Only you see your own room. Access levels are a design tool. Each level says who may depend on a member. Fewer dependents mean easier changes later. Start with private. If a child class needs the member, change it to protected. Make a member public only if the outside world needs it.
points: Protected is open to the class and its children
Private is open to the class only

analogy.title: protected and access control
analogy.body: A family house: the street sees the gate, the family sees the hall, only you see your room

scenes.onScreen: protect.cpp: the derived class reads a protected member
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 5] Everything below this label is open to derived classes. [HL 6] The balance is protected. [HL 9] Savings inherits from Account. [HL 11] Savings can change the protected balance. Interest adds ten percent. [HL 18] Main reads it through a public function. The result is one hundred ten. [HL 5] The label protected opens the members below to the class and its children. [HL 6] The balance starts at one hundred. [HL 11] Savings is a child, so it can change balance. The interest raises it by ten percent. [HL 12] A public getter lets the outside read the value. The answer is one hundred and ten.

scenes.onScreen: a table of the three labels and who can reach them
scenes.animation: Table rows slide in one by one; the row the narrator mentions glows butter
scenes.narration: Read the table row by row. Public is open to all. Protected is open to the class and its children, but closed to outside code. Private is open to the class only. Notice the three rings in the picture. The outer ring is public, the middle ring is protected, and the inner ring is private. The nearer the ring is to the centre, the fewer people can look in.

diagram.caption: a table of the three labels and who can reach them

scenes.onScreen: levels.cpp: one class with public, protected and private data
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 6] Open is public. Everyone can read it. [HL 9] Family is protected. [HL 12] Secret is private. [HL 15] A public getter lets others read the secret. [HL 20] The child adds all three parts. It reads family directly, and secret through the getter. The sum is six. [HL 26] Main may read the public part. [HL 6] The public member is open to everyone. [HL 9] The protected member is open to Child, but not to main. [HL 12] The private member is open only to Base. Child reaches it through the public getter. [HL 20] Sum is one plus two plus three, which gives six.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as levels dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints six, and then one. Notice that main prints the open member, which is one. It cannot touch the other two.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. Public is open to everyone. Two. Protected is open to the class and its children. Three. Private is open to the class only. Four. Choose the strictest label that works. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: Protected is open to the class and its children.
Private is open to the class only.
Choose the strictest label that works.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: Reaching protected data from outside
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the g++ error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. Main reads a protected member. The compiler says the balance is protected within this context. Protected is open to children, not to outside code. Add a public getter. Main is not part of the class family, so protected is closed to it. The compiler says that the member is protected within this context. If main needs the value, add a public function. If main does not need it, leave the member as it is.

scenes.onScreen: Protected is the middle child of access labels. It always gets along with the family.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: Protected is the middle child of access labels. It always gets along with the family.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: pick the right label
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Write a class with a name, an id and a secret code. Decide which label each one needs, and explain in a comment. Hint: the id may be public, the name may be protected, and the secret code should be private. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: virtual functions. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Compiler output (exactly as g++ prints it):

protect.cpp: In function 'int main()':
protect.cpp:11:15: error: 'double Account::balance_' is protected within this context
   11 |     cout << a.balance_ << endl;
      |               ^~~~~~~~
protect.cpp:6:12: note: declared protected here
    6 |     double balance_ = 100;
bug.why: Protected members are for the class and its children. Main is outside code, so it cannot reach them.

pun: "Protected is the middle child of access labels. It always gets along with the family."
challenge: Write a class with a name, an id and a secret code. Decide which label each one needs, and explain in a comment. Hint: the id may be public, the name may be protected, and the secret code should be private.
challengeAnswer: The name can be public through a getter. The id can be protected for derived classes. The secret code stays private.
